ref: Contra Arianos I.15 (NPNF2 section 15; Migne PG 26 Oratio I, sec. 15)
greek: Τὸ δὲ εἶναι τοῦτον τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ Πατρὸς ἴδιον γέννημα ἀρνοῦνται, ὡς μὴ δυναμένου τούτου εἶναι χωρὶς τῆς ἐκ μερῶν καὶ διαιρέσεων ὑπονοίας
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR reads paragraph number as '45.'
english: "But if on the other hand, while they acknowledge with us the name of 'Son,' ... they deny that the Son is the proper offspring of the Father's essence, on the ground that this must imply parts and divisions"
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4, 1892; text as on newadvent)
page: page unknown (NPNF2 vol. 4 printed page not seen; PG 26 column not reliably read)
what_it_says: Athanasius says the Son is the Father's proper offspring of the essence, and that denying this rests on imagining parts and divisions in God.
limits: Says 'proper offspring' but not 'not made' in Athenagoras's sense; Arians would accept the word 'Son' only as a name.

greek: ἀνάγκη λέγειν τὸ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ Πατρὸς ἴδιον αὐτοῦ σύμπαν εἶναι τὸν Υἱόν· τὸ γὰρ ὅλως μετέχεσθαι τὸν Θεὸν, ἴσον ἐστὶ λέγειν, ὅτι καὶ γεννᾷ
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR, gaps in the adjacent Latin column
english: "we are driven to say that what is from the essence of the Father, and proper to Him, is entirely the Son; for it is all one to say that God is wholly participated, and that He begets"
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: What is proper to the Father's essence is wholly the Son, since to be participated is the same as to beget.
limits: Athanasius's language of 'participation' is metaphysical and not a statement about Athenagoras's 'first product'.

greek: οὐχ ἔστιν ἡ Τριὰς ἀΐδιος· ἀλλὰ μονὰς μὲν ἣν πρότερον, ἐκ προσθήκης δὲ γέγονεν ὕστερον Τριάς, καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ χρόνου
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR ('ἢ' for 'ἡ'). This is the word τριάς in Athanasius.
english: "for if the Word is not with the Father from everlasting, the Triad is not everlasting; but a Monad was first, and afterwards by addition it became a Triad"
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: If the Son were not eternal, the Triad would have been a Monad that became a Triad by addition.
limits: Shows Athanasius uses the word 'Triad' against Arians; it does not answer Athenagoras's wording directly.

ref: Contra Arianos I.20 (NPNF2 sec. 20; Migne PG 26 Oratio I)
greek: ὁ Υἱὸς εἰκών ἐστι καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τοῦ Πατρὸς, καὶ χαρακτὴρ, καὶ ἀλήθεια. Εἰ γὰρ ὑπάρχοντος φωτὸς, ἔστιν εἰκὼν αὑτοῦ τὸ ἀπαύγασμα
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR, footnote numbers inline
english: "the Son is the Image and Radiance of the Father, and Expression, and Truth"
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: The Son is Image, Radiance (apaugasma), Expression and Truth of the Father, so an Arian 'once not' is incoherent.
limits: Athanasius uses the 'radiance' image for the Son, while Athenagoras uses 'ray' for the Spirit; the two are not the same role.

ref: Contra Arianos I.21 (NPNF2 sec. 21; Migne PG 26 Oratio I)
greek: ἐφευρεταὶ δυσφημιῶν ἀληθῶς οἱ θεομάχοι ... τομὰς, καὶ ἀποῤῥοίας καὶ ἐπιῤῥοίας καταγοροῦντες κατ᾽ αὐτοῦ
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR ('ἀποῤῥοίας' with rho-breathing as printed)
english: "Who, sooner than confess that the Son is the Father's Image, conceive material and earthly ideas concerning the Father Himself, ascribing to Him severings and effluences and influences."
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: Athanasius rejects 'effluence' (apporroia) as a material image when applied to God, including the Son.
limits: This rejects effluence for the Son; it does not settle the same question for the Spirit in Athenagoras Leg. 10.

ref: Contra Arianos I.22 (NPNF2 sec. 22; Migne PG 26 Oratio I)
greek: οὔτε ὁ Υἱὸς ἐξ ἀποῤῥοίας ἐστὶ τοῦ Πατρὸς ... γεννηθέντος Πατρὸς γεγέννηται
greek_edition: PG 26 (Migne 1857), OCR from archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_026 (no page visible; OCR, verify against scan); OCR with a garbled Latin gap inside the Greek sentence
english: "nor is the Son from effluence of the Father, nor is He begotten from a father that was begotten"
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: The Son is not from an effluence of the Father, and is not begotten from a begotten father.
limits: Denies effluence for the Son only; Athenagoras's Spirit-effluence sentence is not addressed here.

greek_edition: Greek not extracted (PG 26 OCR of the Proverbs passage found at PG 26 offset region but not transcribed); English only
english: "And that creature and offspring are not the same, but differ from each other in nature and the signification of the words, the Lord Himself shows even in the Proverbs."
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: 'Created' and 'begot' in Prov 8:22-25 are distinct; the Wisdom is begotten, not made as a creature.
limits: Refers to the Son as Wisdom; does not treat the Spirit or 'first product' explicitly.

greek_edition: Greek not extracted; English only
english: "For the term 'Only-begotten' is used where there are no brethren, but 'First-born' because of brethren."
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
what_it_says: 'First-born' refers to the Son's condescension to creatures, while 'Only-begotten' names His proper relation to the Father.
limits: Gives Athanasius's own answer to the 'first-born of creation' phrase; not Athenagoras's 'first product' wording.

greek: Οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σύνθεσιν ἀριθμοῦμεν, ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς εἰς πλῆθος ποιούμενοι τὴν παραύξησιν, ἕν καὶ δύο καὶ τρία λέγοντες, οὐδὲ πρῶτον, καὶ δεύτερον, καὶ τρίτον. Υἱὸς γὰρ ἐν τῷ Πατρὶ, καὶ Πατὴρ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ
greek_edition: Migne PG 32 (1857), archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_032; OCR
english: "For we do not count by way of addition, gradually making increase from unity to multitude, and saying one, two, and three — nor yet first, second, and third. ... For the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son"
translator: Blomfield Jackson (NPNF2 vol. 8, 1895)
what_it_says: Basil says the Trinity is not counted by addition or order of numbers; the Son is in the Father, the Father in the Son, with one Monarchy.
limits: Speaks of 'Monarchy' and mutual indwelling; does not use Athenagoras's 'order' (taxis) wording.

greek_edition: Greek not located in PG 32 OCR; English only
english: "Just as when a sunbeam falls on bright and transparent bodies, they themselves become brilliant too ... so souls wherein the Spirit dwells, illuminated by the Spirit, themselves become spiritual, and send forth their grace to others."
translator: Blomfield Jackson (NPNF2 vol. 8, 1895)
what_it_says: The Spirit illuminates souls as a sunbeam does; the image is of illumination, not of a Spirit that is a ray from the Father.
limits: Basil uses 'sun' and 'sunbeam' for the Spirit's operation; he does not discuss the Spirit's substance versus effluence.

ref: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological), sec. VI = Or. 31.6 (NPNF2 sec. VI)
greek: Πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους οὕτω διαλεξόμεθα· τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, ἢ τῶν καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸ ὑφεστηκότων, πάντως ὑποθετέον, ἢ τῶν ἐν ἑτέρῳ θεωρουμένων· ὧν τὸ μὲν, οὐσίαν καλοῦσιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοί, τὸ δὲ, συμβεβηκός. Εἰ μὲν οὖν συμβέβηκεν, ἐνέργεια τοῦτο ἂν εἴη Θεοῦ
greek_edition: Migne PG 36 (1858), archive.org djvu text patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_036; OCR; 'διαλεξόμεθα' printed as 'δ':αλεξόμεθα' in OCR
english: "Now if He were an Accident, He would be an Activity of God, for what else, or of whom else, could He be"
translator: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (NPNF2 vol. 7)
page: PDF page 192 of the NPNF2 vol. 7 scan; printed page unknown
what_it_says: Gregory says the Spirit must be either a substance or an accident; if an accident, He is an activity (energeia) of God and cannot be a person.
limits: Gregory answers the Spirit-as-activity view, which is the strongest objection to reading Leg. 10 'effluence' as a person.

greek_edition: Greek not located in PG 36 OCR (a similar sun/ray sentence found in another oration, not used)
english: "For neither the ray nor the light is another sun, but they are only effulgences from the Sun, and qualities of His essence."
translator: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (NPNF2 vol. 7)
page: PDF page not located by text search (no text match in the layer); printed page unknown
what_it_says: Gregory rejects the sun-and-ray illustration for the Spirit because it suggests composition and makes the Spirit a power not a Person.
limits: Gregory's warning is against sun-ray language for the Spirit, which is precisely what Athenagoras's 'ray' image invites.

greek_edition: Latin not checked; English ANF gives the Greek loan 'προβολαί' (prolations) as printed in the English text
english: "just as the root puts forth the tree, and the fountain the river, and the sun the ray ... the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as ... the apex of the ray is third from the sun."
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3)
what_it_says: Tertullian uses sun-ray and fountain-river analogies for the Son and the Spirit, placing the Spirit third from God and the Son.
limits: Tertullian's ray analogy is the same image Athenagoras uses; it supports an economic procession of the Spirit from the Father through the Son, not a Spirit-effluence.

greek_edition: Latin not checked; English only
english: "three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power"
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3)
what_it_says: The three Persons are one substance and one power, distinguished in degree, form and aspect within the Unity.
limits: Tertullian's 'degree/form/aspect' is the Monarchian-facing version of the Unity-Trinity formula; it is not Nicene vocabulary.

greek_edition: Latin not checked; English only
english: "Sabellius sweeps away the birth of the Son, and then preaches the unity of God ... the revelation of the birth is the mode in which Their unity of nature is manifested to us."
translator: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan (NPNF2 vol. 9, 1899)
page: PDF page 230 of the NPNF2 vol. 9 scan; printed page unknown
what_it_says: Hilary says Sabellius denies the Son's birth and reads the unity of God as an identity of person; the birth is what shows the unity of nature.
limits: Answers Sabellianism, not the Arian reading.

greek_edition: Latin not checked; English only
english: "For of necessity, when we speak what is true, i.e. speak what we know, there is born from the knowledge itself which the memory retains, a word that is altogether of the same kind with that knowledge from which it is born."
translator: Arthur West Haddan (NPNF1 vol. 3, ed. Schaff)
what_it_says: The inner word is born of knowledge and is of the same kind as that knowledge; this is the analogy for the Word born of the Father.
limits: Mind/word analogy; it does not speak of 'idea' as in Athenagoras's Leg. 10 'in idea and in operation'.

greek_edition: Latin not checked; English only
english: "The Word of God, then, the only-begotten Son of the Father, in all things like and equal to the Father, God of God, Light of Light, Wisdom of Wisdom, Essence of Essence"
translator: Arthur West Haddan (NPNF1 vol. 3)
what_it_says: The Word is the Son, equal to the Father and of the same essence, and the Father begets Him as uttering Himself.
limits: Augustine's 'as uttering' is a metaphor; it does not settle whether the Word 'came forth' for creation.

ref: Summa Theologiae I q.15 a.1 (ideas) and a.3
greek_edition: English Summa only; Latin not checked. Correction: the brief said q.14 for ideas; ideas are q.15.
english: "It is necessary to suppose ideas in the divine mind. For the Greek word Idea is in Latin 'forma.'"
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Summa Theologica, 1911-1925; newadvent)
edition: Benziger Brothers (1947 edition, as online at newadvent)
what_it_says: Aquinas holds that God has ideas (exemplar and type) in the divine mind, the 'idea' being the form of things known and made.
limits: Aquinas's ideas are an intellectual exemplar, not Athenagoras's 'idea and energizing power' as a separate subsisting Logos.

ref: Summa Theologiae I q.27 a.1 and a.4
greek_edition: English Summa only; Latin not checked
english: "Some have understood it in the sense of an effect, proceeding from its cause; so Arius took it, saying that the Son proceeds from the Father as His primary creature"
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent)
edition: Benziger Brothers (1947, as online at newadvent)
what_it_says: Aquinas rejects the Arian reading of procession as an effect; procession of the Word is an intelligible operation and the procession of love is 'as spirit', not as begotten.
limits: a.4 says love does not proceed as 'begotten' — this is a Western answer, not Athenagoras's wording.

greek_edition: English Summa only; Latin not checked
english: "the Word of God is only expressive of what is in God the Father, but is both expressive and operative of creatures; and therefore it is said (Psalm 32:9): 'He spake, and they were made'"
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent)
edition: Benziger Brothers (1947, as online at newadvent)
what_it_says: The Word is expressive of the Father and operative toward creatures, which is the Thomist version of Athenagoras's 'idea and energizing power'.
limits: Aquinas keeps the Word's operation as an effect of the one divine act; Athenagoras's 'comes forth' is not reconciled by Aquinas in these words.

greek_edition: English Summa only; Latin not checked
english: "It must be said that the Holy Ghost is from the Son. For if He were not from Him, He could in no wise be personally distinguished from Him"
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (newadvent)
edition: Benziger Brothers (1947, as online at newadvent)
what_it_says: The Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as the Father, otherwise He would not be personally distinct.
limits: Western filioque doctrine; not stated by Athenagoras and not in the Nicene creed text used by the Greek east.

greek_edition: Only a transliteration is in the source (Schaff, Creeds vol. 2, CCEL text): 'to ek tou Patros ekporeuomenon'; Greek letters absent; not transcribed from a Greek edition
english: "who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshiped and glorified"
translator: Philip Schaff (Creeds of Christendom vol. 2, ccel.org text)
edition: Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2 (1877), ccel.org
what_it_says: The 381 creed says the Spirit 'proceedeth from the Father' (no Filioque) and is worshipped with the Father and the Son.
limits: Confirms the Spirit is worshipped, which answers Athenagoras's 'effluence' only partly; Greek letters not checked.
